title: How do you use Porter's five forces to judge an industry in a case?
description: Five forces (Porter) for case interviews. How attractive is this industry? Useful inside market entry and acquisitions.
hook: Porter's five forces is a way of asking how hard it is to make money in an industry. It is useful inside market entry and acquisition cases. Here is a plain-English version you can actually use.
body:
When it helps

How attractive is this industry? Useful inside market entry and acquisitions.

The checklist

Rivalry

  • Number and size of competitors
  • Price wars

New entrants

  • Barriers to entry
  • Capital needed

Substitutes

  • Other ways to meet the need

Buyer power

  • Few big customers?
  • Switching costs

Supplier power

  • Few suppliers?
  • Unique inputs

An example

Should a client buy a chain of independent gyms? Rivalry: lots of gyms compete on price. New entrants: a new gym needs a lease and some equipment, so barriers are fairly low. Substitutes: running, home workouts, fitness apps. Buyer power: members can leave easily. Supplier power: equipment makers have little power. Together that says it is a hard industry to make big profits in, so the client needs a clear edge.

How it sounds in an interview

Before looking at the company itself, I'd like to check how attractive the industry is. I'll look at rivalry, how easy it is to enter, substitutes, and the power of customers and suppliers.

Separate an attractive market from an attractive deal

Consider two imaginary industries. A niche maintenance service has few qualified providers, costly certification and long contracts. A basic delivery service has many competitors, easy switching and customers who compare prices on every order. The first may sustain higher margins, but only if the customers and regulators allow it. The second may struggle to defend price.

Five Forces is a way to form hypotheses about long-run profitability, not a scoring sheet that decides the investment for you. Write down the strongest force and its economic consequence. "High buyer power" is incomplete; "two customers account for 70% of revenue and can demand annual price reductions" is actionable.

For the gym example above, the deeper question is how the target can beat structurally difficult economics. Test site-level occupancy, rent, retention, customer acquisition costs and local differentiation. An industry can be tough overall and still contain a very good operator. Conversely, favourable industry structure does not justify paying any price for a company.
